---
title: Keep copies in sync
description: Sync a record's cached copies whenever a query fetches it.
---

Writing an [entity](/docs/cache/entities) reaches every cached copy, but a
fetch only updates its own query. A todo's detail refetches and shows it
done, while the lists still show it open until they refetch. Entity sync
closes that gap: each fetch writes its copies over the older ones
everywhere. This page shows how to turn it on, which copy wins, and what
it costs.

The examples import `api.ts` and `todos.ts` from
[Getting started](/docs/getting-started), and `entities.ts` from
[Entities](/docs/cache/entities).

## Turn on sync

Give the client the entities to keep in sync:

```ts
import { QueryClient } from "@monarcode/effetch-query";

import { ApiClientLive } from "./api.js";
import { Todos } from "./entities.js";

export const syncedClient = QueryClient.make({
  layer: ApiClientLive,
  entities: { sync: [Todos] },
});
```

With that, when any query's fetch succeeds, each todo in its value is
written over the older copies with the same ID, in every other cached
query whose schema holds `Todo`. No other query fetches, and each one
written keeps its own age, so a stale list still refetches when it's next
used.

## An example

Say an app has a list of the five most recent todos on its home screen, a
detail screen that opens when a todo is tapped, and a page that lists
every todo with an infinite query:

1. The home screen fetches the five todos. Nothing else is cached yet.
2. A tap opens the detail screen. Its placeholder, `Entity.get`, shows the
   list's copy at once, as [Show a placeholder](/docs/queries/placeholders)
   sets up. The detail's fetch lands with the todo done, and the sync
   writes it over the home list's copy. Back on the home screen, the todo
   shows as done.
3. The "all todos" page loads its first page. Its todos are newer than
   the copies cached so far, so the sync writes them over the detail and
   the home list. Loading the next page sends only that page's todos; the
   pages already loaded aren't counted as new.

## Which copy wins

A copy is as new as the fetch it came from, by when that fetch started. A
slow response that lands after a newer one doesn't overwrite it, and the
query that fetched it shows the newer copy instead.

A write is newer still. A write, such as `Entity.set` with a mutation's
result, `Query.set` or a `live` push, counts as newer than every fetch
already in flight, so none of them syncs an older copy over it in another
query. The written query's own fetch is different:

- After `Query.set` or `Entity.set`, a fetch of that query already in
  flight still settles over the write. So after `Entity.set`, a detail
  fetch that was already in flight shows what it fetched.
- A `live` push is applied again to what that fetch returns.

A sync doesn't copy a written todo to other queries either: an entity
write already reached every query that held it, and an optimistic one may
be rolled back.

<Accordions type="multiple">
  <Accordion title="Details: retries, pages, server values and rollbacks">
    A retry counts from when it started. A refetch of an infinite query
    requests its pages one after the other, and each page counts from when
    its own request started.

    A value sent from the server, as
    [Server rendering](/docs/server-rendering) describes, is older than
    any fetch in the browser.

    If a mutation's `optimistic` changed a copy that a newer fetch then
    synced over, and the mutation fails, the rollback puts the synced copy
    back.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

## What syncs

Only a fetch syncs. Writes, `live` pushes and
[stream queries](/docs/queries/streams) don't, so a sync never starts
another sync. A sync updates the todos a query already holds:

- A query that doesn't hold a todo doesn't gain it. A sync never adds a
  row to a list, so invalidate the lists a new todo should join, as with
  `Entity.set`.
- A copy equal to the newer one (`Equal.equals`) isn't written, so its
  readers don't render again.
- Some queries are neither read nor written, and are left to their next
  fetch: one that's invalidated and not in use, that shows a failure,
  that has no value or no schema, that's a stream query, or that opted
  out.

<Accordions type="multiple">
  <Accordion title="Details: dependent queries and errors">
    A fetch doesn't write the queries it read through `ctx.result`, so it
    doesn't start itself again. A query that reads a written query through
    `ctx.result` refetches, as after any write, as
    [Queries that read other queries](/docs/queries/dependent) shows.

    An `id` that throws, or a listener that throws as a query is written,
    is logged with `Effect.logError`. The fetch keeps its value.

  </Accordion>
</Accordions>

## Partial records

A sync replaces copies whole: it writes the newer todo over the older one,
and doesn't combine their fields. If some endpoint's todos are partial,
such as a list whose `decode` fills the fields it doesn't send with
defaults, a fetch of that list writes its partial todos over the full
ones in the cached details. Make every decoded `Todo` complete, or opt the
partial queries out:

```ts
import * as Schema from "effect/Schema";

import { Fetch } from "@monarcode/effetch";

import { Todo } from "./api.js";
import { api } from "./todos.js";

// Served from an index that lags behind the database.
export const indexedTodos = api.query(
  Fetch.endpoint("GET /index/todos", { output: Schema.Array(Todo) }),
  { entities: { sync: false } },
);
```

A query that opts out is left out both ways: its fetches write no other
query, and no other query's fetch writes it. `Entity` writes still reach
it.

`Entity.get` placeholders still help with sync on. A sync runs after a
fetch, and a placeholder fills a detail screen before its first fetch,
from the copy already cached. Use both.

## Cost

Each fetch of a query that holds a synced entity reads every cached query
that holds it, once per synced entity: about one `id` call and one lookup
per cached copy. For a few lists of tens of rows, that's nothing. For an
entity held in many large lists, or a query that polls often, opt out the
queries that don't need it.
